topics.title: Proof-reading: spot it, fix it
topics.intro: Good writers read their work again to find mistakes. Look for capital letters, full stops, question marks, tricky words and word endings. Spot it, then fix it!
topics.teach: Explain how you check a sentence for mistakes, one thing at a time.
topics.talk: Write a sentence with one mistake for {him} to find, then swap: {she} writes one for you.

topics.title: Adding endings in my writing: -ment, -ness, -ful, -less, -ly
topics.intro: Most words stay the same when you add -ment, -ness, -ful, -less or -ly: enjoy → enjoyment. Two rules: a y after a consonant changes to i (happy → happiness), and -le words swap le for ly (gentle → gently). And -ful has only one l!
topics.teach: Explain why happy + ness is spelt “happiness”.
topics.talk: Pick a root word and see how many endings {she} can add: care → careful, careless, carefully.

visual.caption: Usually just add the ending. Watch for y → i, le → ly, and -ful with one l.

topics.title: Spelling: the little words from Years 1 and 2
topics.intro: These are the rest of the tricky words from the Year 1 and Year 2 lists. You use them in nearly every sentence, so they need to be spot on!
topics.teach: Explain the tricky part of “our”, and why “I” is always a capital letter.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to write one sentence using “our”, “your” and “Mrs”.

topics.title: Tricky words in sentences
topics.intro: Now use the tricky words in proper sentences, just like in your own writing. Listen to the word, then write it.
topics.teach: Choose one tricky word and say a new sentence that uses it.
topics.talk: Read one of these sentences aloud for {him} to write on paper, like a little dictation: tricky words and all.

topics.title: Tricky words in sentences 2
topics.intro: More tricky words from the Year 2 list, in sentences from the stories you have read.
topics.teach: Choose one tricky word and say a new sentence that uses it.
topics.talk: Dictate a sentence with two tricky words in it, such as “Who could find the money?”, for {him} to write.

topics.title: Punctuation in my sentences
topics.intro: Punctuation helps your reader. Capital letters start sentences and names (and I). End with . or ? or !. Commas go between things in a list. Apostrophes show missing letters (can’t) or that something belongs to someone (Peter’s jacket).
topics.teach: Explain the difference between “the knights” and “the knight’s shield”.
topics.talk: Spot an apostrophe on a sign or a book cover, and ask {him} what job it is doing.

head: Mark
Its job
rows: Starts a sentence; names, places, days and I
Ends a sentence: telling, asking, or strong feeling
Between things in a list: sticks, string and a torch

items.learn: **any**: The a says “e”: a-n-y.

items.sentence: How ___ pebbles did the crow drop into the jug?
items.explain: Like any: m-a-n-y.
items.learn: **many**: Like any: m-a-n-y.

items.sentence: Peter’s ___ were on the scarecrow.
items.explain: cloth + es: c-l-o-t-h-e-s.
items.learn: **clothes**: cloth + es: c-l-o-t-h-e-s.

items.sentence: The ant was ___ all summer long.
items.explain: The u says “i”: b-u-s-y.
items.learn: **busy**: The u says “i”: b-u-s-y.

items.sentence: The ___ of Brickton were frightened of the dark.
items.explain: peo-ple: e then o.
items.learn: **people**: peo-ple: e then o.

items.sentence: The crow dropped pebbles into the ___.
items.explain: The a says “or”: w-a-t-e-r.
items.learn: **water**: The a says “or”: w-a-t-e-r.

items.sentence: The boy cried “Wolf!” ___, but nobody came.
items.explain: a-g-a-i-n.
items.learn: **again**: a-g-a-i-n.

items.sentence: Rosa cut her sandwich in ___.
items.explain: Silent l: h-a-l-f.
items.learn: **half**: Silent l: h-a-l-f.

items.sentence: People gave ___ to help build more Spitfires.
items.explain: The o says “u”: m-o-n-e-y.
items.learn: **money**: The o says “u”: m-o-n-e-y.

items.sentence: ___ Patel showed Maya a real fossil footprint.
items.clue: a title before a man’s name
items.explain: Short for Mister: capital M, then r.
items.learn: **Mr**: Short for Mister: capital M, then r.

items.sentence: ___ Tabitha Twitchit made hot buttered toast.
items.clue: a title before a married woman’s name
items.explain: Short for Missus: capital M, then r and s.
items.learn: **Mrs**: Short for Missus: capital M, then r and s.

items.sentence: Maya’s ___ waved goodbye at the museum door.
items.explain: par-ents.
items.learn: **parents**: par-ents.

items.sentence: At ___ the dragon lit the fires in the great hall.
items.explain: Capital C, a silent h and a t you don’t hear: Christ-mas.
items.learn: **Christmas**: Capital C, a silent h and a t you don’t hear: Christ-mas.

items.prompt: Which sentence has all the capital letters it needs?

options.text: Maya and Sam went to London on Monday.
Maya and sam went to London on monday.
options.feedback: Sam is a name and Monday is a day: both need capitals.

options.text: maya and Sam went to london on Monday.
options.feedback: Start the sentence with a capital, and London is a place, so it needs one too.

items.explain: Capitals for the start of a sentence, names, places and days of the week.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: Rosa and I raced to the gate.
Rosa and i raced to the gate.
options.feedback: When you write about yourself, I is always a capital.

options.text: rosa and I raced to the gate.
options.feedback: Rosa starts the sentence and is a name: capital R.

items.explain: I is always a capital letter, wherever it is in the sentence.

items.prompt: Which is written as two correct sentences?

options.text: The dragon roared. It was huge.
The dragon roared it was huge.
options.feedback: There are two ideas here. Put a full stop and a capital letter between them.

options.text: The dragon roared. it was huge.
options.feedback: After a full stop, the next sentence starts with a capital letter.

items.explain: Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

items.prompt: Which sentence ends with the right mark?

options.text: Where is the glowing crystal?
Where is the glowing crystal.
options.feedback: It asks something, so it needs a question mark.

options.text: Where is the glowing crystal!
options.feedback: It isn’t an exclamation: it asks a question.

items.explain: A question ends with a question mark.

items.prompt: Which sentence ends with the right mark?

options.text: What a fast car that is!
What a fast car that is?
options.feedback: It starts with What, but it isn’t asking anything: it shows surprise.

options.text: What a fast car that is.
options.feedback: This shows strong feeling, so it needs an exclamation mark.

items.explain: A “What a…” sentence that shows strong feeling is an exclamation: it ends with !

items.prompt: Which one needs a question mark at the end?

options.text: How fast can a cheetah run
How fast that cheetah runs
options.feedback: This shows surprise, so it is an exclamation: How fast that cheetah runs!

options.text: That cheetah runs very fast
options.feedback: This tells you something: it is a statement.

items.explain: Both start with How, but only one asks something you could answer: How fast can a cheetah run?

items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly?

options.text: We need sticks, string and a blanket.
We need sticks string and a blanket.
options.feedback: Put a comma between the first things in the list.

options.text: We need, sticks, string, and, a blanket.
options.feedback: Commas go between the things in the list, not after every word.

items.explain: Use commas between the things in a list, and “and” before the last one.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly?

options.text: Triceratops had horns, a frill and a beak.
Triceratops had horns a frill, and a beak.
options.feedback: The comma goes after “horns”, and no comma is needed before “and”.

options.text: Triceratops had, horns, a frill and a beak.
options.feedback: The list starts after “had”: no comma before horns.

items.explain: horns, a frill and a beak: a comma between the first things, then “and”.

items.prompt: Where does the comma go? “I saw a rocket a planet and a star.”

options.text: after “rocket”
after “planet”
options.feedback: In a simple list, there is no comma before “and”.

options.text: after “saw”
options.feedback: The list starts after “saw”, so no comma there.

items.explain: I saw a rocket, a planet and a star.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

options.text: Can Bleep fix the bolt, the wire and the hatch?
Can Bleep fix the bolt the wire, and the hatch?
options.feedback: The comma goes after “bolt”, and not before “and”.

options.text: can Bleep fix the bolt, the wire and the hatch?
options.feedback: Start the sentence with a capital letter.

options.text: Can Bleep fix the bolt, the wire and the hatch.
options.feedback: It asks something, so it ends with a question mark.

items.explain: Capital letter, commas in the list, and a question mark because it asks something.

items.prompt: Write the short form of the words in bold: “I **could not** find my helmet.”
items.explain: could n(o)t → couldn’t: the apostrophe goes where the o was.

items.prompt: Write the short form of the words in bold: “We **did not** see the wolf.”
items.explain: did n(o)t → didn’t: the apostrophe goes where the o was.

items.prompt: Write the short form of the words in bold: “**It is** time for the race.”
items.explain: It (i)s → It’s: the apostrophe takes the place of the i.

items.prompt: Write the short form of the words in bold: “I **will not** give up!”
items.explain: will not → won’t. This one changes shape, so learn it by heart.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: Peter’s jacket had brass buttons.
Peters jacket had brass buttons.
options.feedback: The jacket belongs to Peter, so add ’s: Peter’s.

options.text: Peters’ jacket had brass buttons.
options.feedback: There is one owner, so the apostrophe goes before the s.

items.explain: Add ’s to show that something belongs to someone: Peter’s jacket.

items.prompt: Which shows that the shield belongs to one knight?

options.text: the knight’s shield
the knights shield
options.feedback: With no apostrophe, it looks like more than one knight.

options.text: the knight’s’ shield
options.feedback: Just one apostrophe, before the s.

items.explain: One knight owns it: the knight’s shield.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: The cars raced round the track.
The car’s raced round the track.
options.feedback: “cars” just means more than one car: a plural needs no apostrophe.

options.text: The cars’ raced round the track.
options.feedback: Nothing belongs to the cars here, so there is no apostrophe.

items.explain: Never use an apostrophe just to make a plural.
